'''Bruce Nathan Ames''' (December 16, 1928 – October 5, 2024) was an American biochemist who was a professor of [[biochemistry]] and Molecular Biology Emeritus at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], and was a senior scientist at [[Children's Hospital Oakland Research Institute]] (CHORI).<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.chori.org/Principal_Investigators/Ames_Bruce/ames_overview.html |title= Biography and information |work= CHORI |access-date= 2008-09-13 |archive-date= 2017-12-13 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171213142752/http://www.chori.org/Principal_Investigators/Ames_Bruce/ames_overview.html }}</ref> Ames made contributions to understanding the mechanisms of mutagenesis and DNA repair. He invented the [[Ames test]], a widely used assay for easily and cheaply evaluating the [[mutagenicity]] of compounds.<ref name="nytimes"/>  The test revolutionized the field of toxicology and has played a crucial role in identifying numerous environmental and industrial carcinogens.

==Biography==
Ames, raised in [[New York City]], was a graduate of the [[Bronx High School of Science]]. His undergraduate studies were at [[Cornell University]] in [[Ithaca, New York]], and his graduate studies were completed at the [[California Institute of Technology]].<ref>{{cite journal |author=Ames BN |title=An enthusiasm for metabolism |journal=Journal of Biological Chemistry |volume=278 |issue=7 |pages=4369–80 |date=February 2003 |doi=10.1074/jbc.X200010200 |pmid=12496254|doi-access=free }}</ref>
[[File:Bruce Ames.jpg|thumb|left|Ames in 2003]]
Ames was elected a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1970.<ref name=AAAS>{{cite web|title=Book of Members, 1780–2010: Chapter A|url=http://www.amacad.org/publications/BookofMembers/ChapterA.pdf|publisher=American Academy of Arts and Sciences|access-date=17 April 2011}}</ref> He is a recipient of the [[The Franklin Institute Awards|Bolton S. Corson Medal]] in 1980, [[Tyler Prize for Environmental Achievement]] in 1985, the [[Japan Prize]] in 1997, the [[National Medal of Science]] in 1998 and the [[Thomas Hunt Morgan Medal]] in 2004,<ref>{{cite journal|last=Smith|first=Gerald R|author2=Johnston Mark|date=February 2004|title=The 2004 Thomas Hunt Morgan Medal|journal=[[Genetics (journal)|Genetics]]|volume=166|issue=2|pages=645–6|issn=0016-6731|pmid=15020453|doi=10.1534/genetics.166.2.645|pmc=1470756}}</ref> among many others.

Ames' research focused on cancer and aging and he authored over 550 scientific publications. He is among the few hundred most-cited scientists in all fields.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bruceames.org |title=About Dr. Ames|work=Bruce Ames official website }}</ref>

Ames' later research included identifying agents that delay the mitochondrial decay of aging, understanding the role of mitochondrial decay in aging, particularly in the brain, optimizing micronutrient intakes in the population to prevent disease, malnutrition, and obesity. He was also interested in mutagens as they relate to cancer prevention and aging.<ref>[http://mcb.berkeley.edu/faculty/BMB/amesb.html Bruce N. Ames]. University of California</ref>

Ames received more than $650,000 in support from the [[National Foundation for Cancer Research]] between 1998 and 2007.<ref>{{cite journal|pmc=1505022|year=2001|title=National Foundation for Cancer Research|journal=Neoplasia|volume=3|issue=1|pages=88–90|doi=10.1038/sj.neo.7900130|last1=Salisbury|first1=Franklin}}</ref>

He was married to Giovanna Ferro-Luzzi Ames, who was also a professor of biochemistry at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=DeMarini |first=David M. |date=2024-11-01 |title=Bruce Nathan Ames: A scientist to remember (December 16, 1928—October 5, 2024) |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S1383571824001086 |journal=Mutation Research/Genetic Toxicology and Environmental Mutagenesis |volume=900 |article-number=503832 |doi=10.1016/j.mrgentox.2024.503832 |bibcode=2024MRGTE.90003832D |issn=1383-5718|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Ames died on October 5, 2024 at a hospital in [[Berkeley, California]] at the age of 95.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sanders |first=Robert |date=2024-10-10 |title=Bruce Ames, developer of a simple, widely used test to detect carcinogens, is dead at 95 |url=https://news.berkeley.edu/2024/10/10/bruce-ames-developer-of-a-simple-widely-used-test-to-detect-carcinogens-is-dead-at-95/ |access-date=2024-10-12 |website=Berkeley News |language=en}}</ref>

==Ames on synthetic carcinogens==
In the 1970s, Ames developed the [[Ames test]] which is a cheap and convenient assay for [[mutagen]]s and therefore potential [[carcinogen]]s.  Previous carcinogenic testing used live animals, and the procedures are expensive and time-consuming. This made animal testing impractical for use in screening on a wide scale, and reduced the number of compounds that could be tested.  The Ames test on the other hand uses the bacteria ''[[Salmonella typhimurium]]'' to test for mutagens, and is considerably cheaper and faster. The Ames test became widely used as an initial screen for possible carcinogens and has been used to identify potential carcinogens previously used in commercial products.<ref>{{Cite journal
| last1 = Ames | first1 = B. N. | author-link1 = Bruce Ames
| title = Identifying environmental chemicals causing mutations and cancer
| journal = [[Science (journal)|Science]]
| volume = 204
| issue = 4393
| pages = 587–593
| year = 1979
| url = http://legacy.library.ucsf.edu/documentStore/e/p/c/epc74e00/Sepc74e00.pdf
| pmid = 373122
| jstor = 1748159
| doi=10.1126/science.373122
| bibcode = 1979Sci...204..587A }}</ref> Their identification led to some of those formulations, such as chemicals used in  hair dye,<ref>{{cite journal|last=Ames|first=Bruce|author2=Kammen H.O.|date=June 1975|title=Hair Dyes Are Mutagenic: Identification of a Variety of Mutagenic Ingredients|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|doi=10.1073/pnas.72.6.2423|volume=72|issue=6|pages=2423–2427|pmc=432771|pmid=1094469|bibcode=1975PNAS...72.2423A|doi-access=free}}</ref> being withdrawn from commercial use.   The ease with which Ames test allows widely used chemicals to be identified as possible carcinogens made him an early hero of environmentalism.<ref name="nytimes"/>

Subsequent work in Ames' lab involved looking at an overview of what was mutagenic or carcinogenic, and to what degree. Previously, scientists tended to only look for positive or negative results without considering the magnitude of the effect, which meant that as more and more items were shown to be potentially mutagenic, there was no system for evaluating the relative dangers. He also continued to test various natural and man-made compounds,  and discovered that, despite what he and others had assumed, naturally occurring compounds were not turning out to be benign as compared to man-made ones. His continued work eventually led to his falling out of favor with many environmentalists.  As natural chemicals turned out to also be frequently mutagenic, he argued that environmental exposure to manufactured chemicals may be of limited relevance to human cancer, even when such chemicals are mutagenic in an Ames test and carcinogenic in rodent assays.<ref>{{Cite journal
| last1 = Forman | first1 = D.
| title = Ames, the Ames test, and the causes of cancer
| journal = BMJ (Clinical Research Ed.)
| volume = 303
| issue = 6800
| pages = 428–429
| year = 1991
| pmid = 1912830
| pmc = 1670593
| doi=10.1136/bmj.303.6800.428
}}</ref>  He contended that most human genetic damage arises from essential micronutrients lacking in poor diets and the oxidation of DNA during normal metabolism, and that the most important environmental carcinogens may include some whose chief effect is to cause the chronic division of stem cells whereby the normal protective mechanisms of a cell become less effective.

He argued against the banning of synthetic pesticides and other chemicals such as [[Daminozide|Alar]] which have been shown to be carcinogenic. Ames published results showing that many ordinary food products would be found carcinogenic according to the same criteria.<ref name="nytimes">[http://tierneylab.blogs.nytimes.com/2007/06/06/synthetic-v-natural-pesticides/ Synthetic v. Natural Pesticides]. ''New York Times'' (June 6, 2007)</ref><ref>Gold, L.S., Slone, T.H., Ames, B.N., and Manley, N.B., Pesticide Residues in Food and Cancer Risk: A Critical Analysis. In: Handbook of Pesticide Toxicology, Second Edition (R. Krieger, ed.), San Diego, CA: Academic Press, pp. 799-843 (2001)</ref> Ames was concerned that overzealous attention to the relatively minor health effects of trace quantities of carcinogens may divert scarce financial resources away from major health risks, and cause public confusion about the relative importance of different hazards. Ames considered himself a leading "contrarian in the hysteria over tiny traces of chemicals that may or may not cause cancer", and said that "if you have thousands of hypothetical risks that you are supposed to pay attention to, that completely drives out the major risks you should be aware of."<ref>{{Cite journal
| last1 = Twombly | first1 = R.
| title = Federal carcinogen report debuts new list of nominees
| journal = Journal of the National Cancer Institute
| volume = 93
| issue = 18
| page = 1372
| year = 2001
| pmid = 11562386
| doi=10.1093/jnci/93.18.1372
| doi-access = free
}}</ref>
